A cookie without Domain belongs only to the host that set it, and localhost has no dot and so no eTLD+1, so Domain=localhost is ignored. Two dev setups that work are at the end."}],["$","link","2",{"rel":"canonical","href":"/v2/samesite-and-the-subdomain-cookie-bug"}]],"error":null,"digest":"$undefined"}

13:I[86734,["7654","static/chunks/7654-2fe46cddc56d2856.js","9489","static/chunks/app/v2/%5Bslug%5D/page-2e406f5eec6a5c88.js"],"MdDoc"]
14:T697c,<p>You log in at <code>localhost:3000</code>, and the server sets a session cookie. Then you open <code>thembase.localhost:3000</code>. Same machine, same browser, same port, but the cookie is gone and the server says you're not logged in.</p>
<p>The first suspect is usually <code>SameSite</code>, but switching it to <code>Lax</code>, <code>Strict</code> or <code>None</code> changes nothing. So where did the cookie go?</p>
<h2>How the browser decides whether to send a cookie</h2>
<p>One scene runs through the article: an office building with many companies in it.</p>





























<table><thead><tr><th>Building</th><th>Browser</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>a department's front desk</td><td>a host, such as <code>www.example.com</code></td></tr><tr><td>a company that owns several desks</td><td>a site, such as <code>example.com</code></td></tr><tr><td>an access card a desk gives you</td><td>a cookie</td></tr><tr><td>the building directory, listing names that belong to the building itself, not to a company</td><td>the Public Suffix List</td></tr><tr><td>a rule printed on the card: show it when another company brings you over, or not</td><td><code>SameSite</code></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>The browser holds your cards. Each time you walk up to a desk, it picks the cards that desk recognizes. Here is how it picks.</p>
<h3>Host</h3>
<p>The host is the part of the URL after <code>://</code> and before the port.</p>
<ul>
<li>The host of <code>http://localhost:3000</code> is <code>localhost</code>.</li>
<li>The host of <code>http://thembase.localhost:3000</code> is <code>thembase.localhost</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p>Same port and same machine don't matter: to the browser these are two different hosts, two different desks in the building.</p>
<h3>Which hosts a cookie is sent to</h3>
<p>When a server sets a cookie with <code>Set-Cookie</code>, the browser records which hosts the cookie belongs to. On every later request, it attaches only the cookies that belong to that request's host.</p>
<p>Say the server at <code>myapp.test</code> returns one of these headers, and the browser then sends requests to two hosts:</p>




















<table><thead><tr><th>Header from <code>myapp.test</code></th><th>Request to <code>myapp.test</code></th><th>Request to <code>sub.myapp.test</code></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>Set-Cookie: id=1</code></td><td>sent</td><td><strong>not sent</strong></td></tr><tr><td><code>Set-Cookie: id=1; Domain=myapp.test</code></td><td>sent</td><td>sent</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>A cookie without <code>Domain</code> is <strong>host-only</strong>: it belongs only to the host that set it, and not even its subdomains get it. In building terms, a card from one desk works only at that desk. With <code>Domain=myapp.test</code>, the card works at every desk of the company.</p>
<h3><code>Domain</code> can't be too wide: the Public Suffix List</h3>
<p><code>Domain</code> can only name the host itself or a name above it, so <code>sub.myapp.test</code> can write <code>Domain=myapp.test</code>. But what if the name above is shared by many people?</p>
<p><code>youraccount.github.io</code> and <code>myaccount.github.io</code> are two different people's sites. If <code>youraccount.github.io</code> could set a cookie with <code>Domain=github.io</code>, the browser would send it to every <code>*.github.io</code>, mine included.</p>
<p>The <a href="https://publicsuffix.org/">Public Suffix List</a> (PSL) is the directory that prevents this. It lists domains anyone can register names under, such as <code>com</code>, <code>co.uk</code>, <code>github.io</code> and <code>vercel.app</code>. These are public suffixes: the building itself, not a company. <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis/">RFC 6265bis</a> §5.7 step 9 says that when <code>Domain</code> is a public suffix:</p>
<ul>
<li>if it equals the host, the browser ignores <code>Domain</code> and the cookie becomes host-only;</li>
<li>otherwise, the browser drops the whole cookie.</li>
</ul>
<p>So <code>Domain=github.io</code> from <code>youraccount.github.io</code> is dropped. Nobody can issue a card for the whole building.</p>
<p>The browser looks up the end of a host on the list. The part it finds is the eTLD (effective top-level domain). For <code>www.example.com</code>:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>com</code>: on the list, so it is the eTLD, the building itself</li>
<li><code>example.com</code>: the eTLD plus one more name to the left, <code>example</code>, called the eTLD+1. This is the site, the company in the building</li>
<li><code>www.example.com</code>: the full host, one desk of that company</li>
</ul>
<p>If nothing is found on the list, the browser takes the rightmost dot-separated name as the eTLD. So an eTLD isn't always on the list: the eTLD of <code>shop.unknowntld</code> is <code>unknowntld</code>, which the list doesn't contain.</p>



































<table><thead><tr><th>Domain</th><th>Found on the list</th><th>eTLD</th><th>eTLD+1 (site)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>www.example.com</code></td><td><code>com</code></td><td><code>com</code></td><td><code>example.com</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>blog.example.co.uk</code></td><td><code>co.uk</code></td><td><code>co.uk</code></td><td><code>example.co.uk</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>youraccount.github.io</code></td><td><code>github.io</code></td><td><code>github.io</code></td><td><code>youraccount.github.io</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>shop.unknowntld</code></td><td>nothing</td><td><code>unknowntld</code></td><td><code>shop.unknowntld</code></td></tr></tbody></table>
<h3><code>SameSite</code>: requests started by another site</h3>
<p>Host, <code>Domain</code> and the PSL together decide <strong>which hosts a cookie belongs to</strong>. Now suppose the cookie does belong to the host a request is going to, but the request was started by a page on another site. The browser then reads the cookie's <code>SameSite</code>. For example, if the server set the cookie with <code>SameSite=Strict</code>, this request goes out without it.</p>
<p>So the browser first has to tell whether the page and the request's URL are the same site. Same site is not the same as same origin:</p>



































<table><thead><tr><th></th><th>Same Site</th><th>Same Origin</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Used by</td><td>the <code>SameSite</code> cookie attribute, the <code>Sec-Fetch-Site</code> header</td><td>the Same-Origin Policy (storage, fetch, postMessage)</td></tr><tr><td>Compares</td><td>eTLD+1, plus the scheme in Chrome 91 and later</td><td>scheme, host and port, all exact</td></tr><tr><td><code>www.example.com</code> vs <code>blog.example.com</code></td><td>same site</td><td>different origin</td></tr><tr><td><code>http://x.com</code> vs <code>https://x.com</code></td><td>same site by the old definition, cross-site in Chrome 91 and later</td><td>different origin</td></tr><tr><td><code>example.com:80</code> vs <code>example.com:8080</code></td><td>same site</td><td>different origin</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>In the building, same origin is the same desk through the same door; same site is the same company.</p>
<h2>Back to localhost: why the cookie doesn't arrive</h2>
<p>The cookie that was set:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">{</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  httpOnly</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">true</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  secure</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">false</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  sameSite</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">"lax"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  path</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">"/"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>There is no <code>Domain</code>, so the cookie is host-only and belongs only to <code>localhost</code>. <code>thembase.localhost</code> is a different host, so the browser doesn't attach the cookie to requests going there.</p>
<h3>What about adding <code>Domain=localhost</code>?</h3>
<p>That doesn't work either. <code>localhost</code> is a name reserved by <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6761">RFC 6761</a> §6.3 and isn't on the PSL. It has no dot, so its rightmost name is <code>localhost</code> itself, and that is its eTLD. An eTLD+1 needs one more name to the left of the eTLD, and <code>localhost</code> has nothing to its left, so it has no eTLD+1:</p>
<pre><code>www.example.com      eTLD = com          eTLD+1 = example.com
shop.unknowntld      eTLD = unknowntld   eTLD+1 = shop.unknowntld
thembase.localhost   eTLD = localhost    eTLD+1 = thembase.localhost
localhost            eTLD = localhost    eTLD+1 = (none)
</code></pre>
<p>Whenever a host has no eTLD+1, <code>Domain</code> can only be the host itself and the cookie can only be host-only. IP addresses and <code>co.uk</code> itself have no eTLD+1 either, so the same rule applies to them. Neither browser's code has a rule specific to <code>localhost</code>:</p>
<ul>
<li>Chrome finds no eTLD+1 for <code>localhost</code> (<code>net/cookies/cookie_util.cc</code>).</li>
<li>Firefox needs one more name to the left of <code>localhost</code> before there is an eTLD+1, as in <code>thembase.localhost</code>. Bare <code>localhost</code> returns <code>NS_ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_DOMAIN_LEVELS</code>, and on that error the cookie code only accepts a <code>Domain</code> identical to the host (<code>netwerk/cookie/CookieCommons.cpp</code>).</li>
</ul>
<p>So <code>Domain=localhost</code> is ignored and the cookie stays host-only. In building terms, <code>localhost</code> is the lobby. The lobby has a desk, but it isn't a company; <code>thembase.localhost</code> is a company in the building.</p>
<p>Measured on Chrome 156 and Firefox 155:</p>





















































<table><thead><tr><th>Set on</th><th>Attributes</th><th>Stored as</th><th>Did the subdomain get it?</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>localhost</code></td><td>no <code>Domain</code></td><td>belongs to <code>localhost</code> only</td><td>no, <code>thembase.localhost</code> got nothing</td></tr><tr><td><code>localhost</code></td><td><code>Domain=localhost</code></td><td>belongs to <code>localhost</code> only</td><td>no</td></tr><tr><td><code>localhost</code></td><td><code>Domain=.localhost</code></td><td>belongs to <code>localhost</code> only</td><td>no</td></tr><tr><td><code>thembase.localhost</code></td><td><code>Domain=localhost</code></td><td>dropped</td><td>—</td></tr><tr><td><code>thembase.localhost</code></td><td><code>Domain=thembase.localhost</code></td><td><code>thembase.localhost</code> and its subdomains</td><td>yes, <code>a.thembase.localhost</code> got it</td></tr><tr><td><code>myapp.test</code></td><td>no <code>Domain</code></td><td>belongs to <code>myapp.test</code> only</td><td>no</td></tr><tr><td><code>myapp.test</code></td><td><code>Domain=myapp.test</code></td><td><code>myapp.test</code> and its subdomains</td><td>yes, <code>sub.myapp.test</code> got it</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p><code>Domain=localhost</code> and <code>Domain=.localhost</code> raise no error. The browser keeps the cookie and ignores <code>Domain</code>, so everything looks fine on <code>localhost</code>, and the cookie only turns out to be missing on another host.</p>
<h3>Why changing <code>SameSite</code> doesn't help</h3>
<p><code>SameSite</code> only decides whether a cookie that already belongs to a host is attached. This cookie never belonged to <code>thembase.localhost</code>, so no <code>SameSite</code> value changes anything. With <code>Lax</code>, <code>Strict</code>, <code>None; Secure</code>, or no <code>SameSite</code> at all, the <code>localhost</code> cookie never reached <code>thembase.localhost</code>.</p>
<p><code>localhost</code> and <code>thembase.localhost</code> are still two different sites, though. Following a link from one to the other, Chrome and Firefox both sent <code>Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site</code>. In Chrome, a <code>fetch()</code> from <code>thembase.localhost</code> to <code>localhost</code> also carried only <code>SameSite=None</code> cookies. So <code>SameSite</code> does apply between them; it just isn't why the cookie went missing.</p>
<h2>Fixing the localhost dev setup</h2>
<p>Bare <code>localhost</code> is the lobby and can't issue a card for a whole company. Use a name that has an eTLD+1, such as <code>myapp.test</code>. Either of these works.</p>
<p><strong>1. <code>myapp.test</code> via <code>/etc/hosts</code>.</strong> RFC 6761 reserves <code>.test</code> for exactly this, and unlike <code>.local</code> it doesn't collide with macOS mDNS. Point the names at loopback:</p>
<pre><code># /etc/hosts
127.0.0.1   myapp.test
127.0.0.1   sub.myapp.test
</code></pre>
<p>Or in one line:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="bash" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="bash" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">echo</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> "127.0.0.1 myapp.test sub.myapp.test"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49"> |</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> sudo</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> tee</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> -a</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> /etc/hosts</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>Develop at <code>http://myapp.test:3000</code> and set the cookie with <code>Domain=myapp.test</code>; both hosts get it. <code>myapp.test</code> behaves like a production <code>myapp.com</code>.</p>
<p>One catch: <code>myapp.test</code> over plain HTTP is not a secure context, and cookies with <code>Secure</code> are dropped there. Chrome 156 and Firefox 155 dropped <code>Secure</code>, <code>Secure; SameSite=Lax</code> and <code>SameSite=None; Secure</code> cookies set over <code>http://myapp.test</code>, and kept the same cookies set over <code>https://myapp.test</code>. If your production cookies are <code>Secure</code>, run the dev server on HTTPS with a local certificate.</p>
<p><strong>2. <code>myapp.localhost</code> and <code>sub.myapp.localhost</code>, no <code>/etc/hosts</code> needed.</strong> Chrome and Firefox both resolve any <code>*.localhost</code> name to loopback themselves. <code>myapp.localhost</code> is a company in the building, so a cookie set there with <code>Domain=myapp.localhost</code> reaches <code>sub.myapp.localhost</code>. <code>thembase.localhost</code> in the table above has the same structure, and its cookie reached <code>a.thembase.localhost</code> in Chrome 156 and Firefox 151 and 155. Safari wasn't tested.</p>
<p>Two things look like fixes and aren't:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>Domain=.localhost</code> or <code>Domain=localhost</code>.</strong> The browser ignores the attribute, and the subdomain still gets nothing.</li>
<li><strong><code>SameSite=None; Secure</code>.</strong> <code>SameSite</code> never makes a cookie belong to more hosts.</li>
</ul>
<h2>SameSite in detail</h2>
<h3>The three values</h3>
<pre><code>Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=Strict
Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=Lax
Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=None; Secure
</code></pre>

























<table><thead><tr><th>Value</th><th>Cross-site subresource request (<code>&#x3C;img></code>, <code>&#x3C;iframe></code>, <code>fetch</code>)</th><th>Cross-site top-level navigation</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Strict</td><td>not sent</td><td><strong>Not sent.</strong> Even following a link from another site to yours, the first request has no cookie</td></tr><tr><td>Lax</td><td>not sent</td><td><strong>Sent for GET</strong> (following a link). A cross-site POST form is not sent</td></tr><tr><td>None</td><td>sent, but Firefox stores it per top-level site (see below)</td><td>sent. Requires <code>Secure</code></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>A <strong>top-level navigation</strong> changes the URL in the address bar: following a link, following a redirect, submitting a form. <code>&#x3C;img src></code>, <code>&#x3C;iframe></code>, <code>&#x3C;script></code>, <code>fetch()</code> and XHR don't change the address bar; those are subresource requests.</p>
<p>With a bank's session cookie set to <code>Lax</code>:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Sent.</strong> The user clicks a link to the bank in an email. That is a top-level GET navigation, so the user arrives logged in.</li>
<li><strong>Not sent.</strong> An attacker's page includes <code>&#x3C;img src="https://yourbank.com/transfer?to=evil"></code>. That is a subresource request, so it goes out without the session cookie and the CSRF fails. A hidden form that POSTs to your site is a top-level navigation, but not a GET, so <code>Lax</code> doesn't send it either.</li>
</ul>
<p><code>Strict</code> is the most conservative: even an email link lands logged out. Keep it for high-risk actions such as an admin panel or a bank's transfer confirmation.</p>
<h3>When <code>SameSite</code> is missing</h3>
<p>Only Chrome treats a cookie with no <code>SameSite</code> as <code>Lax</code> (since Chrome 80); Firefox and Safari treat it as <code>None</code> (<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie#browser_compatibility">MDN compat data</a>). With Firefox's Total Cookie Protection turned off (<code>network.cookie.cookieBehavior=0</code>), Firefox 151 and 155 sent a cookie with no <code>SameSite</code> on a cross-site <code>&#x3C;img></code> request; Chrome 156 didn't. So write <code>SameSite=Lax</code> explicitly.</p>
<p>Chrome has one exception for such cookies: for the first two minutes after one is set, it is still sent on a cross-site top-level POST (RFC 6265bis calls this Lax-allowing-unsafe). On Chrome 156, the cookie went out on a cross-site POST 16 seconds after it was set and not 147 seconds after. A cookie with an explicit <code>SameSite=Lax</code> was sent neither time.</p>
<h3>Firefox stores <code>None</code> cookies separately per site</h3>
<p>Ad networks use <code>SameSite=None</code> cookies to recognize the same person. Say news.test and shop.test both show ads from ads.test. While the user browses news.test, ads.test sets a cookie <code>id=42</code>. Later the user browses shop.test, the browser sends <code>id=42</code> back to ads.test, and ads.test knows the same person visited both sites.</p>
<p>Firefox's ad <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E2AoYIKwJqM">It's time to come back to Firefox</a> brings back a group of early internet celebrities to dance together, and it is about how good the old internet was. The ad sells a feeling, but Firefox also changed a setting: since June 2022, Total Cookie Protection has been on by default for all desktop users. In Mozilla's words, trackers used to be able to link one person's behavior across many sites. With the feature on, ads.test treats the user on news.test and the user on shop.test as two unrelated people (<a href="https://blog.mozilla.org/en/mozilla/firefox-rolls-out-total-cookie-protection-by-default-to-all-users-worldwide/">Mozilla</a>).</p>
<p>Chrome also planned to stop third-party cookies, but after years of delays, Google announced in April 2025 that it would keep the current approach. Third-party cookies are still sent, and users who want them off have to turn them off in settings (<a href="https://privacysandbox.google.com/blog/privacy-sandbox-next-steps">Privacy Sandbox</a>).</p>
<p>Firefox's approach is to store cookies separately by which site the user was on at the time. The cookie ads.test set on news.test is sent only while the user is on news.test:</p>




















<table><thead><tr><th>User is browsing</th><th>Cookie Chrome sends to ads.test</th><th>Cookie Firefox sends to ads.test</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>news.test</td><td><code>id=42</code></td><td><code>id=42</code></td></tr><tr><td>shop.test</td><td><code>id=42</code></td><td>none</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>That table only illustrates the rule; the ads.test case was not measured. The case below was measured, and Firefox follows the same rule:</p>
<p>myapp.test makes a chat widget, and other.test embeds it in its own page. The user first logs in on myapp.test and gets myapp.test's login cookie, then browses other.test. When other.test's page sends a request to myapp.test:</p>















<table><thead><tr><th></th><th>Chrome 156</th><th>Firefox 155</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Sends the cookie from the myapp.test login</td><td>yes</td><td>no</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>The user got the login cookie while browsing myapp.test, so Firefox sends it only while the user is browsing myapp.test. If the widget relies on that cookie to know who is logged in, it shows as logged out in Firefox when embedded on other.test.</p>
<p>Following a link, though, makes Firefox send more. In the measurement, the user clicked a link on a localhost page to thembase.localhost, then thembase.localhost's page sent a request to localhost. By the rule above, the user is now browsing thembase.localhost and localhost's cookies shouldn't go along, but Firefox 155 sent them. The no-SameSite and <code>SameSite=None</code> cookies were sent; the <code>Lax</code> and <code>Strict</code> ones still were not, because the request is still cross-site. This exception was measured only on *.localhost.</p>
<p>Firefox probably does this for flows like "log in to site B with your site A account". The user follows a link from A to B, B's page asks A whether this person is logged in, and if that request carries no A cookie, A can only answer "not logged in".</p>
<h3>Are http and https the same site: Schemeful same-site</h3>
<pre><code>Address bar: http://myapp.test
GET https://myapp.test/api
→ Cookie: id=abc     Firefox 155 (the cookie is SameSite=Lax)
→ (no Cookie)        Chrome 156
</code></pre>
<p>The domain is the same; only the page is http and the request is https. Since version 91, Chrome compares the scheme (http or https) too when deciding whether two sides are the same site, so Chrome treats this request as cross-site and sends neither <code>Lax</code> nor <code>Strict</code> cookies. Firefox compares only the eTLD+1 and treats it as same-site. The change is called <a href="https://web.dev/articles/schemeful-samesite">Schemeful Same-Site</a>. Serving the whole site over HTTPS avoids the case.</p>
<h2>Why SameSite=None requires Secure</h2>
<p>A <code>SameSite=None</code> cookie goes out on cross-site requests too, so it is sent far more often. Without <code>Secure</code> it would also travel over plain HTTP, where anyone on the same coffee-shop Wi-Fi could read it off the network. So browsers that enforce the rule reject such cookies outright:</p>
<pre><code>Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=None             rejected, no Secure
Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=None; Secure     accepted, sent over HTTPS only
</code></pre>
<p>Chrome has enforced this since Chrome 80, Firefox since Firefox 131, and Safari doesn't enforce it (<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie#browser_compatibility">MDN compat data</a>). Measured: Chrome 156 and Firefox 151 and 155 all rejected <code>SameSite=None</code> without <code>Secure</code>.</p>
<h2>The current best combination</h2>
<pre><code>Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>HttpOnly</code></strong>: JavaScript on the page can't read it from <code>document.cookie</code>, so an XSS payload can't copy the session ID out. XSS can still send requests from the page, though, and the browser still attaches the cookie to them.</li>
<li><strong><code>Secure</code></strong>: HTTPS only. Chrome and Firefox accept it on <code>http://localhost</code> too.</li>
<li><strong><code>SameSite=Lax</code></strong>: written out, because only Chrome defaults to it.</li>
<li><strong><code>Path=/</code></strong>: the whole app.</li>
</ul>
<p>Add <code>Domain</code> only when subdomains really need to share the cookie. Once you do, every subdomain gets it, including ones run by other teams or other programs.</p>

You log in at `localhost:3000`, and the server sets a session cookie. Then you open `thembase.localhost:3000`. Same machine, same browser, same port, but the cookie is gone and the server says you're not logged in.

The first suspect is usually `SameSite`, but switching it to `Lax`, `Strict` or `None` changes nothing. So where did the cookie go?

## How the browser decides whether to send a cookie

One scene runs through the article: an office building with many companies in it.

| Building | Browser |
|---|---|
| a department's front desk | a host, such as `www.example.com` |
| a company that owns several desks | a site, such as `example.com` |
| an access card a desk gives you | a cookie |
| the building directory, listing names that belong to the building itself, not to a company | the Public Suffix List |
| a rule printed on the card: show it when another company brings you over, or not | `SameSite` |

The browser holds your cards. Each time you walk up to a desk, it picks the cards that desk recognizes. Here is how it picks.

### Host

The host is the part of the URL after `://` and before the port.

- The host of `http://localhost:3000` is `localhost`.
- The host of `http://thembase.localhost:3000` is `thembase.localhost`.

Same port and same machine don't matter: to the browser these are two different hosts, two different desks in the building.

### Which hosts a cookie is sent to

When a server sets a cookie with `Set-Cookie`, the browser records which hosts the cookie belongs to. On every later request, it attaches only the cookies that belong to that request's host.

Say the server at `myapp.test` returns one of these headers, and the browser then sends requests to two hosts:

| Header from `myapp.test` | Request to `myapp.test` | Request to `sub.myapp.test` |
|---|---|---|
| `Set-Cookie: id=1` | sent | **not sent** |
| `Set-Cookie: id=1; Domain=myapp.test` | sent | sent |

A cookie without `Domain` is **host-only**: it belongs only to the host that set it, and not even its subdomains get it. In building terms, a card from one desk works only at that desk. With `Domain=myapp.test`, the card works at every desk of the company.

### `Domain` can't be too wide: the Public Suffix List

`Domain` can only name the host itself or a name above it, so `sub.myapp.test` can write `Domain=myapp.test`. But what if the name above is shared by many people?

`youraccount.github.io` and `myaccount.github.io` are two different people's sites. If `youraccount.github.io` could set a cookie with `Domain=github.io`, the browser would send it to every `*.github.io`, mine included.

The [Public Suffix List](https://publicsuffix.org/) (PSL) is the directory that prevents this. It lists domains anyone can register names under, such as `com`, `co.uk`, `github.io` and `vercel.app`. These are public suffixes: the building itself, not a company. [RFC 6265bis](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis/) §5.7 step 9 says that when `Domain` is a public suffix:

- if it equals the host, the browser ignores `Domain` and the cookie becomes host-only;
- otherwise, the browser drops the whole cookie.

So `Domain=github.io` from `youraccount.github.io` is dropped. Nobody can issue a card for the whole building.

The browser looks up the end of a host on the list. The part it finds is the eTLD (effective top-level domain). For `www.example.com`:

- `com`: on the list, so it is the eTLD, the building itself
- `example.com`: the eTLD plus one more name to the left, `example`, called the eTLD+1. This is the site, the company in the building
- `www.example.com`: the full host, one desk of that company

If nothing is found on the list, the browser takes the rightmost dot-separated name as the eTLD. So an eTLD isn't always on the list: the eTLD of `shop.unknowntld` is `unknowntld`, which the list doesn't contain.

| Domain | Found on the list | eTLD | eTLD+1 (site) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `www.example.com` | `com` | `com` | `example.com` |
| `blog.example.co.uk` | `co.uk` | `co.uk` | `example.co.uk` |
| `youraccount.github.io` | `github.io` | `github.io` | `youraccount.github.io` |
| `shop.unknowntld` | nothing | `unknowntld` | `shop.unknowntld` |

### `SameSite`: requests started by another site

Host, `Domain` and the PSL together decide **which hosts a cookie belongs to**. Now suppose the cookie does belong to the host a request is going to, but the request was started by a page on another site. The browser then reads the cookie's `SameSite`. For example, if the server set the cookie with `SameSite=Strict`, this request goes out without it.

So the browser first has to tell whether the page and the request's URL are the same site. Same site is not the same as same origin:

| | Same Site | Same Origin |
|---|---|---|
| Used by | the `SameSite` cookie attribute, the `Sec-Fetch-Site` header | the Same-Origin Policy (storage, fetch, postMessage) |
| Compares | eTLD+1, plus the scheme in Chrome 91 and later | scheme, host and port, all exact |
| `www.example.com` vs `blog.example.com` | same site | different origin |
| `http://x.com` vs `https://x.com` | same site by the old definition, cross-site in Chrome 91 and later | different origin |
| `example.com:80` vs `example.com:8080` | same site | different origin |

In the building, same origin is the same desk through the same door; same site is the same company.

## Back to localhost: why the cookie doesn't arrive

The cookie that was set:

```js
{
  httpOnly: true,
  secure: false,
  sameSite: "lax",
  path: "/",
}
```

There is no `Domain`, so the cookie is host-only and belongs only to `localhost`. `thembase.localhost` is a different host, so the browser doesn't attach the cookie to requests going there.

### What about adding `Domain=localhost`?

That doesn't work either. `localhost` is a name reserved by [RFC 6761](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6761) §6.3 and isn't on the PSL. It has no dot, so its rightmost name is `localhost` itself, and that is its eTLD. An eTLD+1 needs one more name to the left of the eTLD, and `localhost` has nothing to its left, so it has no eTLD+1:

```
www.example.com      eTLD = com          eTLD+1 = example.com
shop.unknowntld      eTLD = unknowntld   eTLD+1 = shop.unknowntld
thembase.localhost   eTLD = localhost    eTLD+1 = thembase.localhost
localhost            eTLD = localhost    eTLD+1 = (none)
```

Whenever a host has no eTLD+1, `Domain` can only be the host itself and the cookie can only be host-only. IP addresses and `co.uk` itself have no eTLD+1 either, so the same rule applies to them. Neither browser's code has a rule specific to `localhost`:

- Chrome finds no eTLD+1 for `localhost` (`net/cookies/cookie_util.cc`).
- Firefox needs one more name to the left of `localhost` before there is an eTLD+1, as in `thembase.localhost`. Bare `localhost` returns `NS_ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_DOMAIN_LEVELS`, and on that error the cookie code only accepts a `Domain` identical to the host (`netwerk/cookie/CookieCommons.cpp`).

So `Domain=localhost` is ignored and the cookie stays host-only. In building terms, `localhost` is the lobby. The lobby has a desk, but it isn't a company; `thembase.localhost` is a company in the building.

Measured on Chrome 156 and Firefox 155:

| Set on | Attributes | Stored as | Did the subdomain get it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `localhost` | no `Domain` | belongs to `localhost` only | no, `thembase.localhost` got nothing |
| `localhost` | `Domain=localhost` | belongs to `localhost` only | no |
| `localhost` | `Domain=.localhost` | belongs to `localhost` only | no |
| `thembase.localhost` | `Domain=localhost` | dropped | — |
| `thembase.localhost` | `Domain=thembase.localhost` | `thembase.localhost` and its subdomains | yes, `a.thembase.localhost` got it |
| `myapp.test` | no `Domain` | belongs to `myapp.test` only | no |
| `myapp.test` | `Domain=myapp.test` | `myapp.test` and its subdomains | yes, `sub.myapp.test` got it |

`Domain=localhost` and `Domain=.localhost` raise no error. The browser keeps the cookie and ignores `Domain`, so everything looks fine on `localhost`, and the cookie only turns out to be missing on another host.

### Why changing `SameSite` doesn't help

`SameSite` only decides whether a cookie that already belongs to a host is attached. This cookie never belonged to `thembase.localhost`, so no `SameSite` value changes anything. With `Lax`, `Strict`, `None; Secure`, or no `SameSite` at all, the `localhost` cookie never reached `thembase.localhost`.

`localhost` and `thembase.localhost` are still two different sites, though. Following a link from one to the other, Chrome and Firefox both sent `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site`. In Chrome, a `fetch()` from `thembase.localhost` to `localhost` also carried only `SameSite=None` cookies. So `SameSite` does apply between them; it just isn't why the cookie went missing.

## Fixing the localhost dev setup

Bare `localhost` is the lobby and can't issue a card for a whole company. Use a name that has an eTLD+1, such as `myapp.test`. Either of these works.

**1. `myapp.test` via `/etc/hosts`.** RFC 6761 reserves `.test` for exactly this, and unlike `.local` it doesn't collide with macOS mDNS. Point the names at loopback:

```
# /etc/hosts
127.0.0.1   myapp.test
127.0.0.1   sub.myapp.test
```

Or in one line:

```bash
echo "127.0.0.1 myapp.test sub.myapp.test" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
```

Develop at `http://myapp.test:3000` and set the cookie with `Domain=myapp.test`; both hosts get it. `myapp.test` behaves like a production `myapp.com`.

One catch: `myapp.test` over plain HTTP is not a secure context, and cookies with `Secure` are dropped there. Chrome 156 and Firefox 155 dropped `Secure`, `Secure; SameSite=Lax` and `SameSite=None; Secure` cookies set over `http://myapp.test`, and kept the same cookies set over `https://myapp.test`. If your production cookies are `Secure`, run the dev server on HTTPS with a local certificate.

**2. `myapp.localhost` and `sub.myapp.localhost`, no `/etc/hosts` needed.** Chrome and Firefox both resolve any `*.localhost` name to loopback themselves. `myapp.localhost` is a company in the building, so a cookie set there with `Domain=myapp.localhost` reaches `sub.myapp.localhost`. `thembase.localhost` in the table above has the same structure, and its cookie reached `a.thembase.localhost` in Chrome 156 and Firefox 151 and 155. Safari wasn't tested.

Two things look like fixes and aren't:

- **`Domain=.localhost` or `Domain=localhost`.** The browser ignores the attribute, and the subdomain still gets nothing.
- **`SameSite=None; Secure`.** `SameSite` never makes a cookie belong to more hosts.

## SameSite in detail

### The three values

```
Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=Strict
Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=Lax
Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=None; Secure
```

| Value | Cross-site subresource request (`<img>`, `<iframe>`, `fetch`) | Cross-site top-level navigation |
|---|---|---|
| Strict | not sent | **Not sent.** Even following a link from another site to yours, the first request has no cookie |
| Lax | not sent | **Sent for GET** (following a link). A cross-site POST form is not sent |
| None | sent, but Firefox stores it per top-level site (see below) | sent. Requires `Secure` |

A **top-level navigation** changes the URL in the address bar: following a link, following a redirect, submitting a form. `<img src>`, `<iframe>`, `<script>`, `fetch()` and XHR don't change the address bar; those are subresource requests.

With a bank's session cookie set to `Lax`:

- **Sent.** The user clicks a link to the bank in an email. That is a top-level GET navigation, so the user arrives logged in.
- **Not sent.** An attacker's page includes `<img src="https://yourbank.com/transfer?to=evil">`. That is a subresource request, so it goes out without the session cookie and the CSRF fails. A hidden form that POSTs to your site is a top-level navigation, but not a GET, so `Lax` doesn't send it either.

`Strict` is the most conservative: even an email link lands logged out. Keep it for high-risk actions such as an admin panel or a bank's transfer confirmation.

### When `SameSite` is missing

Only Chrome treats a cookie with no `SameSite` as `Lax` (since Chrome 80); Firefox and Safari treat it as `None` ([MDN compat data](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie#browser_compatibility)). With Firefox's Total Cookie Protection turned off (`network.cookie.cookieBehavior=0`), Firefox 151 and 155 sent a cookie with no `SameSite` on a cross-site `<img>` request; Chrome 156 didn't. So write `SameSite=Lax` explicitly.

Chrome has one exception for such cookies: for the first two minutes after one is set, it is still sent on a cross-site top-level POST (RFC 6265bis calls this Lax-allowing-unsafe). On Chrome 156, the cookie went out on a cross-site POST 16 seconds after it was set and not 147 seconds after. A cookie with an explicit `SameSite=Lax` was sent neither time.

### Firefox stores `None` cookies separately per site

Ad networks use `SameSite=None` cookies to recognize the same person. Say news.test and shop.test both show ads from ads.test. While the user browses news.test, ads.test sets a cookie `id=42`. Later the user browses shop.test, the browser sends `id=42` back to ads.test, and ads.test knows the same person visited both sites.

Firefox's ad [It's time to come back to Firefox](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E2AoYIKwJqM) brings back a group of early internet celebrities to dance together, and it is about how good the old internet was. The ad sells a feeling, but Firefox also changed a setting: since June 2022, Total Cookie Protection has been on by default for all desktop users. In Mozilla's words, trackers used to be able to link one person's behavior across many sites. With the feature on, ads.test treats the user on news.test and the user on shop.test as two unrelated people ([Mozilla](https://blog.mozilla.org/en/mozilla/firefox-rolls-out-total-cookie-protection-by-default-to-all-users-worldwide/)).

Chrome also planned to stop third-party cookies, but after years of delays, Google announced in April 2025 that it would keep the current approach. Third-party cookies are still sent, and users who want them off have to turn them off in settings ([Privacy Sandbox](https://privacysandbox.google.com/blog/privacy-sandbox-next-steps)).

Firefox's approach is to store cookies separately by which site the user was on at the time. The cookie ads.test set on news.test is sent only while the user is on news.test:

| User is browsing | Cookie Chrome sends to ads.test | Cookie Firefox sends to ads.test |
|---|---|---|
| news.test | `id=42` | `id=42` |
| shop.test | `id=42` | none |

That table only illustrates the rule; the ads.test case was not measured. The case below was measured, and Firefox follows the same rule:

myapp.test makes a chat widget, and other.test embeds it in its own page. The user first logs in on myapp.test and gets myapp.test's login cookie, then browses other.test. When other.test's page sends a request to myapp.test:

| | Chrome 156 | Firefox 155 |
|---|---|---|
| Sends the cookie from the myapp.test login | yes | no |

The user got the login cookie while browsing myapp.test, so Firefox sends it only while the user is browsing myapp.test. If the widget relies on that cookie to know who is logged in, it shows as logged out in Firefox when embedded on other.test.

Following a link, though, makes Firefox send more. In the measurement, the user clicked a link on a localhost page to thembase.localhost, then thembase.localhost's page sent a request to localhost. By the rule above, the user is now browsing thembase.localhost and localhost's cookies shouldn't go along, but Firefox 155 sent them. The no-SameSite and `SameSite=None` cookies were sent; the `Lax` and `Strict` ones still were not, because the request is still cross-site. This exception was measured only on *.localhost.

Firefox probably does this for flows like "log in to site B with your site A account". The user follows a link from A to B, B's page asks A whether this person is logged in, and if that request carries no A cookie, A can only answer "not logged in".

### Are http and https the same site: Schemeful same-site

```
Address bar: http://myapp.test
GET https://myapp.test/api
→ Cookie: id=abc     Firefox 155 (the cookie is SameSite=Lax)
→ (no Cookie)        Chrome 156
```

The domain is the same; only the page is http and the request is https. Since version 91, Chrome compares the scheme (http or https) too when deciding whether two sides are the same site, so Chrome treats this request as cross-site and sends neither `Lax` nor `Strict` cookies. Firefox compares only the eTLD+1 and treats it as same-site. The change is called [Schemeful Same-Site](https://web.dev/articles/schemeful-samesite). Serving the whole site over HTTPS avoids the case.

## Why SameSite=None requires Secure

A `SameSite=None` cookie goes out on cross-site requests too, so it is sent far more often. Without `Secure` it would also travel over plain HTTP, where anyone on the same coffee-shop Wi-Fi could read it off the network. So browsers that enforce the rule reject such cookies outright:

```
Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=None             rejected, no Secure
Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=None; Secure     accepted, sent over HTTPS only
```

Chrome has enforced this since Chrome 80, Firefox since Firefox 131, and Safari doesn't enforce it ([MDN compat data](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie#browser_compatibility)). Measured: Chrome 156 and Firefox 151 and 155 all rejected `SameSite=None` without `Secure`.

## The current best combination

```
Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
```

- **`HttpOnly`**: JavaScript on the page can't read it from `document.cookie`, so an XSS payload can't copy the session ID out. XSS can still send requests from the page, though, and the browser still attaches the cookie to them.
- **`Secure`**: HTTPS only. Chrome and Firefox accept it on `http://localhost` too.
- **`SameSite=Lax`**: written out, because only Chrome defaults to it.
- **`Path=/`**: the whole app.

Add `Domain` only when subdomains really need to share the cookie. Once you do, every subdomain gets it, including ones run by other teams or other programs.

16:T684c,:T6953,<p>在 <code>localhost:3000</code> 登入，server 設了一個 session cookie。接著打開 <code>thembase.localhost:3000</code>，同一台機器、同一個瀏覽器、同一個 port，cookie 卻不見了，server 說你沒登入。</p>
<p>第一個懷疑的通常是 <code>SameSite</code>，可是把它改成 <code>Lax</code>、<code>Strict</code>、<code>None</code>，結果都一樣。那 cookie 到底是怎麼不見的呢？</p>
<h2>瀏覽器怎麼決定要不要帶 cookie</h2>
<p>整篇用同一個場景：一棟辦公大樓，裡面有很多家公司。</p>





























<table><thead><tr><th>大樓</th><th>瀏覽器</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>某個部門的櫃台</td><td>host，例如 <code>www.example.com</code></td></tr><tr><td>擁有好幾個櫃台的公司</td><td>site，例如 <code>example.com</code></td></tr><tr><td>櫃台發給你的門禁卡</td><td>cookie</td></tr><tr><td>大樓的名冊，列出哪些名字是大樓本身、不是公司</td><td>Public Suffix List</td></tr><tr><td>印在卡上的規則：別家公司帶你過來的時候，要不要出示這張卡</td><td><code>SameSite</code></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>瀏覽器替你保管這些卡。你每次走到一個櫃台，它就從口袋裡挑出這個櫃台認得的卡出示。下面一個一個看，它是怎麼挑的。</p>
<h3>host</h3>
<p>host 是網址裡 <code>://</code> 後面、port 前面的名字。</p>
<ul>
<li><code>http://localhost:3000</code> 的 host 是 <code>localhost</code>。</li>
<li><code>http://thembase.localhost:3000</code> 的 host 是 <code>thembase.localhost</code>。</li>
</ul>
<p>port 一樣、機器一樣都沒有用，對瀏覽器來說，這是兩個不同的 host，也就是大樓裡兩個不同的櫃台。</p>
<h3>cookie 會送給哪些 host</h3>
<p>server 用 <code>Set-Cookie</code> 設 cookie 的時候，瀏覽器會一起記下這個 cookie 屬於哪些 host。之後每發一個請求，只帶上屬於那個 host 的 cookie。</p>
<p>假設 <code>myapp.test</code> 的 server 回了下面兩種 header，瀏覽器接著對兩個 host 發請求：</p>




















<table><thead><tr><th><code>myapp.test</code> 回的 header</th><th>送到 <code>myapp.test</code></th><th>送到 <code>sub.myapp.test</code></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>Set-Cookie: id=1</code></td><td>帶</td><td><strong>不帶</strong></td></tr><tr><td><code>Set-Cookie: id=1; Domain=myapp.test</code></td><td>帶</td><td>帶</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>沒寫 <code>Domain</code> 的 cookie 叫 <strong>host-only</strong>，它只屬於設它的 host，subdomain 也收不到。換成大樓的說法，櫃台發的卡只能在這個櫃台用。加了 <code>Domain=myapp.test</code>，這張卡就變成整家公司的櫃台都能用。</p>
<h3><code>Domain</code> 不能寫太大：Public Suffix List</h3>
<p><code>Domain</code> 只能寫 host 本身或它上層的名字，所以 <code>sub.myapp.test</code> 可以寫 <code>Domain=myapp.test</code>。可是如果上層的名字是大家共用的呢？</p>
<p><code>youraccount.github.io</code> 跟 <code>myaccount.github.io</code> 是兩個不同人的網站。如果 <code>youraccount.github.io</code> 可以設一個 <code>Domain=github.io</code> 的 cookie，瀏覽器就會把它送給每一個 <code>*.github.io</code>，連我的網站也收得到。</p>
<p><a href="https://publicsuffix.org/">Public Suffix List</a>（PSL）就是用來防這件事的名冊。它列出大家都能在底下註冊名字的網域，像 <code>com</code>、<code>co.uk</code>、<code>github.io</code>、<code>vercel.app</code>，這些叫 public suffix，也就是大樓本身，不是一家公司。<a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis/">RFC 6265bis</a> §5.7 第 9 步規定瀏覽器碰到 <code>Domain</code> 是 public suffix 的時候：</p>
<ul>
<li>跟 host 一模一樣的話，忽略 <code>Domain</code>，cookie 變成 host-only。</li>
<li>跟 host 不一樣的話，整個 cookie 丟掉。</li>
</ul>
<p>所以 <code>youraccount.github.io</code> 設的 <code>Domain=github.io</code> 會被丟掉，誰都不能發一張整棟大樓通用的卡。</p>
<p>瀏覽器拿 host 的結尾去名冊上查，查到的部分叫 eTLD（effective top-level domain）。以 <code>www.example.com</code> 來說：</p>
<ul>
<li><code>com</code>：名冊上有，所以是 eTLD，大樓本身</li>
<li><code>example.com</code>：eTLD 往左多接一個名字 <code>example</code>，叫 eTLD+1。這就是 site，也就是大樓裡的那家公司</li>
<li><code>www.example.com</code>：完整的 host，那家公司的某一個櫃台</li>
</ul>
<p>名冊上查不到的話，瀏覽器就把用點隔開的最右邊那個名字當成 eTLD。所以 eTLD 不一定在名冊上，<code>shop.unknowntld</code> 的 eTLD 就是名冊上沒有的 <code>unknowntld</code>。</p>



































<table><thead><tr><th>網域</th><th>名冊上查到</th><th>eTLD</th><th>eTLD+1（site）</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>www.example.com</code></td><td><code>com</code></td><td><code>com</code></td><td><code>example.com</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>blog.example.co.uk</code></td><td><code>co.uk</code></td><td><code>co.uk</code></td><td><code>example.co.uk</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>youraccount.github.io</code></td><td><code>github.io</code></td><td><code>github.io</code></td><td><code>youraccount.github.io</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>shop.unknowntld</code></td><td>沒有</td><td><code>unknowntld</code></td><td><code>shop.unknowntld</code></td></tr></tbody></table>
<h3><code>SameSite</code>：別的網站發起的請求要不要帶</h3>
<p>host、<code>Domain</code> 跟 PSL 一起決定 cookie <strong>屬於哪些 host</strong>。假設 cookie 已經屬於請求要去的那個 host，可是這個請求是從別的 site 的頁面發起的，這時瀏覽器會再讀 cookie 上的 <code>SameSite</code>。比如 server 設 cookie 時寫了 <code>SameSite=Strict</code>，這個請求就不會帶它。</p>
<p>所以瀏覽器要先判斷發起請求的頁面跟請求要去的網址是不是同站。同站跟同源（same origin）不一樣：</p>



































<table><thead><tr><th></th><th>同站（Same Site）</th><th>同源（Same Origin）</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>誰在用</td><td><code>SameSite</code> cookie 屬性、<code>Sec-Fetch-Site</code> header</td><td>Same-Origin Policy（storage、fetch、postMessage）</td></tr><tr><td>比較什麼</td><td>eTLD+1，Chrome 91 起再加上 scheme</td><td>scheme、host、port 三個都要一樣</td></tr><tr><td><code>www.example.com</code> 對 <code>blog.example.com</code></td><td>同站</td><td>不同源</td></tr><tr><td><code>http://x.com</code> 對 <code>https://x.com</code></td><td>舊定義算同站，Chrome 91 起算跨站</td><td>不同源</td></tr><tr><td><code>example.com:80</code> 對 <code>example.com:8080</code></td><td>同站</td><td>不同源</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>用大樓來講，同源是同一個櫃台、從同一個門進來；同站是同一家公司。</p>
<h2>回到 localhost：cookie 為什麼帶不過去</h2>
<p>當時設的 cookie 長這樣：</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">{</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  httpOnly</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">true</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  secure</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">false</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  sameSite</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">"lax"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  path</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">"/"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>這裡沒有 <code>Domain</code>，所以它是 host-only，只屬於 <code>localhost</code>。<code>thembase.localhost</code> 是另一個 host，瀏覽器對它發請求時當然不會帶。</p>
<h3>那加上 <code>Domain=localhost</code> 呢？</h3>
<p>也不行。<code>localhost</code> 是 <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6761">RFC 6761</a> §6.3 保留的名字，不在 PSL 上。它沒有點，最右邊的名字就是 <code>localhost</code> 本身，所以 eTLD 是 <code>localhost</code>。eTLD+1 要在 eTLD 左邊多接一個名字，<code>localhost</code> 左邊沒有名字可接，因此沒有 eTLD+1：</p>
<pre><code>www.example.com      eTLD = com          eTLD+1 = example.com
shop.unknowntld      eTLD = unknowntld   eTLD+1 = shop.unknowntld
thembase.localhost   eTLD = localhost    eTLD+1 = thembase.localhost
localhost            eTLD = localhost    eTLD+1 = （沒有）
</code></pre>
<p>只要 host 沒有 eTLD+1，<code>Domain</code> 就只能寫跟 host 一樣的值，cookie 也只能是 host-only。IP 位址跟 <code>co.uk</code> 本身也沒有 eTLD+1，所以也走這條規則。兩個瀏覽器的程式碼裡，都沒有專門判斷 <code>localhost</code> 的規則：</p>
<ul>
<li>Chrome 找不到 <code>localhost</code> 的 eTLD+1（<code>net/cookies/cookie_util.cc</code>）。</li>
<li>Firefox 要 <code>localhost</code> 左邊再接一個名字才有 eTLD+1，例如 <code>thembase.localhost</code>。單獨的 <code>localhost</code> 會回傳 <code>NS_ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_DOMAIN_LEVELS</code>，cookie 的程式碰到這個錯誤，就只接受跟 host 一模一樣的 <code>Domain</code>（<code>netwerk/cookie/CookieCommons.cpp</code>）。</li>
</ul>
<p>所以 <code>Domain=localhost</code> 會被忽略，cookie 還是 host-only。換成大樓的說法，<code>localhost</code> 是大樓的大廳，大廳有櫃台，可是它不是一家公司；<code>thembase.localhost</code> 才是大樓裡的一家公司。</p>
<p>Chrome 156 跟 Firefox 155 的實測結果：</p>





















































<table><thead><tr><th>在哪裡設</th><th>屬性</th><th>瀏覽器存成</th><th>subdomain 有沒有收到</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>localhost</code></td><td>沒有 <code>Domain</code></td><td>只屬於 <code>localhost</code></td><td>沒有，<code>thembase.localhost</code> 收不到</td></tr><tr><td><code>localhost</code></td><td><code>Domain=localhost</code></td><td>只屬於 <code>localhost</code></td><td>沒有</td></tr><tr><td><code>localhost</code></td><td><code>Domain=.localhost</code></td><td>只屬於 <code>localhost</code></td><td>沒有</td></tr><tr><td><code>thembase.localhost</code></td><td><code>Domain=localhost</code></td><td>整個丟掉</td><td>—</td></tr><tr><td><code>thembase.localhost</code></td><td><code>Domain=thembase.localhost</code></td><td><code>thembase.localhost</code> 跟它的 subdomain</td><td>有，<code>a.thembase.localhost</code> 收到了</td></tr><tr><td><code>myapp.test</code></td><td>沒有 <code>Domain</code></td><td>只屬於 <code>myapp.test</code></td><td>沒有</td></tr><tr><td><code>myapp.test</code></td><td><code>Domain=myapp.test</code></td><td><code>myapp.test</code> 跟它的 subdomain</td><td>有，<code>sub.myapp.test</code> 收到了</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p><code>Domain=localhost</code> 跟 <code>Domain=.localhost</code> 不會報錯。瀏覽器留下 cookie、忽略 <code>Domain</code>，所以在 <code>localhost</code> 上一切正常，換到別的 host 才發現 cookie 不見了。</p>
<h3>為什麼改 <code>SameSite</code> 沒用</h3>
<p><code>SameSite</code> 只決定已經屬於這個 host 的 cookie 要不要帶。這個 cookie 從一開始就不屬於 <code>thembase.localhost</code>，<code>SameSite</code> 設成什麼都改變不了。實測時 <code>Lax</code>、<code>Strict</code>、<code>None; Secure</code> 跟不寫，<code>localhost</code> 的 cookie 都沒有送到 <code>thembase.localhost</code>。</p>
<p>不過 <code>localhost</code> 跟 <code>thembase.localhost</code> 確實是兩個不同的站。從其中一個點連結到另一個，Chrome 跟 Firefox 送出的都是 <code>Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site</code>。在 Chrome 裡，從 <code>thembase.localhost</code> 對 <code>localhost</code> 發 <code>fetch()</code>，也只會帶上 <code>SameSite=None</code> 的 cookie。所以 <code>SameSite</code> 在它們之間是有作用的，只是 cookie 不見不是它造成的。</p>
<h2>修好 localhost 的開發環境</h2>
<p>單獨一個 <code>localhost</code> 是大廳，沒辦法發整家公司通用的卡。換成一個有 eTLD+1 的名字就可以，例如 <code>myapp.test</code>，下面兩種都行。</p>
<p><strong>1. 用 <code>/etc/hosts</code> 設 <code>myapp.test</code>。</strong> RFC 6761 保留 <code>.test</code> 就是為了這種用途，它也不像 <code>.local</code> 會跟 macOS 的 mDNS 撞名。把名字指到 loopback：</p>
<pre><code># /etc/hosts
127.0.0.1   myapp.test
127.0.0.1   sub.myapp.test
</code></pre>
<p>或是一行加進去：</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="bash" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="bash" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">echo</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> "127.0.0.1 myapp.test sub.myapp.test"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49"> |</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> sudo</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> tee</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> -a</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62"> /etc/hosts</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>開發時用 <code>http://myapp.test:3000</code>，cookie 加上 <code>Domain=myapp.test</code>，兩個 host 就都收得到。<code>myapp.test</code> 的行為跟正式環境的 <code>myapp.com</code> 一樣。</p>
<p>要留意的是，走純 HTTP 的 <code>myapp.test</code> 不是 secure context，帶 <code>Secure</code> 的 cookie 在這裡會被丟掉。在 <code>http://myapp.test</code> 設的 <code>Secure</code>、<code>Secure; SameSite=Lax</code>、<code>SameSite=None; Secure</code> 三種 cookie，Chrome 156 跟 Firefox 155 都丟了；同樣的 cookie 改在 <code>https://myapp.test</code> 設，兩邊都收下。如果正式環境的 cookie 有 <code>Secure</code>，開發用的 server 就要用本機憑證跑 HTTPS。</p>
<p><strong>2. 用 <code>myapp.localhost</code> 跟 <code>sub.myapp.localhost</code>，不必改 <code>/etc/hosts</code>。</strong> Chrome 跟 Firefox 都會自己把 <code>*.localhost</code> 解析到 loopback。<code>myapp.localhost</code> 是大樓裡的一家公司，所以在它上面設 cookie、加上 <code>Domain=myapp.localhost</code>，<code>sub.myapp.localhost</code> 就收得到。上面表格的 <code>thembase.localhost</code> 就是同樣的結構，在 Chrome 156、Firefox 151 跟 155 都送到了 <code>a.thembase.localhost</code>。Safari 沒有測。</p>
<p>另外有兩種做法看起來像解法，其實沒用：</p>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>Domain=.localhost</code> 或 <code>Domain=localhost</code>。</strong> 瀏覽器會忽略這個屬性，subdomain 還是收不到。</li>
<li><strong><code>SameSite=None; Secure</code>。</strong> <code>SameSite</code> 不會讓 cookie 屬於更多 host。</li>
</ul>
<h2>SameSite 的細節</h2>
<h3>三個值</h3>
<pre><code>Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=Strict
Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=Lax
Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=None; Secure
</code></pre>

























<table><thead><tr><th>值</th><th>跨站的 subresource 請求（<code>&#x3C;img></code>、<code>&#x3C;iframe></code>、<code>fetch</code>）</th><th>跨站的 top-level navigation</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Strict</td><td>不送</td><td><strong>不送。</strong> 從別的網站點連結到你的網站，第一個請求也不帶 cookie</td></tr><tr><td>Lax</td><td>不送</td><td><strong>GET 會送</strong>（例如點連結）。跨站的 POST 表單不送</td></tr><tr><td>None</td><td>送，但 Firefox 會照 top-level site 分開存（見下方）</td><td>送。必須加 <code>Secure</code></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p><strong>top-level navigation</strong> 會改變網址列上的網址，例如點連結、跟著 redirect、送出表單。<code>&#x3C;img src></code>、<code>&#x3C;iframe></code>、<code>&#x3C;script></code>、<code>fetch()</code>、XHR 都不會改網址列，這些是 subresource 請求。</p>
<p>銀行網站的 session cookie 設成 <code>Lax</code> 時：</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>會送。</strong> 使用者在 email 裡點了銀行的連結。這是 top-level navigation，方法是 GET，所以打開銀行網站時還是登入狀態。</li>
<li><strong>不送。</strong> 攻擊者在自己的頁面放一個 <code>&#x3C;img src="https://yourbank.com/transfer?to=evil"></code>，這是 subresource 請求，送出去時沒有 session cookie，CSRF 就失敗了。藏起來的表單用 POST 送到你的網站，雖然算 top-level navigation，可是方法不是 GET，<code>Lax</code> 一樣不送。</li>
</ul>
<p><code>Strict</code> 最保守，連 email 連結點進去都是登出狀態，留給管理後台或銀行的轉帳確認這種風險高的操作。</p>
<h3>沒寫 <code>SameSite</code> 的時候</h3>
<p>只有 Chrome 會把沒寫 <code>SameSite</code> 的 cookie 當成 <code>Lax</code>（Chrome 80 開始），Firefox 跟 Safari 當成 <code>None</code>（<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie#browser_compatibility">MDN 相容性資料</a>）。把 Firefox 的 Total Cookie Protection 關掉（<code>network.cookie.cookieBehavior=0</code>）的話，Firefox 151 跟 155 會在跨站的 <code>&#x3C;img></code> 請求帶上沒寫 <code>SameSite</code> 的 cookie，Chrome 156 不會。所以 <code>SameSite=Lax</code> 要明寫出來。</p>
<p>Chrome 對沒寫的 cookie 還有一個例外：設下去之後的前兩分鐘，跨站的 top-level POST 還是會送（RFC 6265bis 叫它 Lax-allowing-unsafe）。在 Chrome 156 上，cookie 設下去 16 秒後，跨站 POST 有帶它，147 秒後就沒帶了。明寫 <code>SameSite=Lax</code> 的 cookie 兩次都沒帶。</p>
<h3>Firefox 會把 <code>None</code> 的 cookie 分開存</h3>
<p>廣告商靠 <code>SameSite=None</code> 的 cookie 認出同一個人。news.test 跟 shop.test 都放了 ads.test 的廣告，使用者逛 news.test 時，ads.test 設了一個 cookie <code>id=42</code>。之後使用者逛 shop.test，瀏覽器又把 <code>id=42</code> 送回 ads.test，ads.test 就知道這兩個網站是同一個人逛的。</p>
<p>Firefox 的宣傳片 <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E2AoYIKwJqM">It's time to come back to Firefox</a> 找回一群早期的網路紅人一起跳舞，講的是以前的網路有多美好。廣告打的是情懷，不過 Firefox 在設定上也真的有動作：從 2022 年 6 月起，所有桌面版使用者預設都開著 Total Cookie Protection。照 Mozilla 的說明，追蹤者原本能把同一個人在好幾個網站上的行為串起來。開了這個功能之後，ads.test 就會把 news.test 上跟 shop.test 上的使用者當成兩個不相關的人（<a href="https://blog.mozilla.org/en/mozilla/firefox-rolls-out-total-cookie-protection-by-default-to-all-users-worldwide/">Mozilla</a>）。</p>
<p>Chrome 原本也打算停用第三方 cookie，可是拖了幾年之後，Google 在 2025 年 4 月宣布維持現狀。第三方 cookie 照樣送出，使用者想關掉的話，得自己去設定裡關（<a href="https://privacysandbox.google.com/blog/privacy-sandbox-next-steps">Privacy Sandbox</a>）。</p>
<p>Firefox 的做法是把 cookie 照「使用者當時在哪個網站上」分開放。ads.test 在 news.test 上設的 cookie，只有使用者在 news.test 上時才會送出去：</p>




















<table><thead><tr><th>使用者正在逛</th><th>Chrome 送給 ads.test 的 cookie</th><th>Firefox 送給 ads.test 的 cookie</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>news.test</td><td><code>id=42</code></td><td><code>id=42</code></td></tr><tr><td>shop.test</td><td><code>id=42</code></td><td>沒有</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>上面這張表只是說明原理，ads.test 的例子沒有實測。下面這個情況有實測，Firefox 也照同一個規則處理：</p>
<p>myapp.test 做了一個聊天小工具，other.test 把它嵌在自己的頁面上。使用者先在 myapp.test 登入，拿到 myapp.test 的登入 cookie，之後再去逛 other.test。other.test 的頁面向 myapp.test 發請求時：</p>















<table><thead><tr><th></th><th>Chrome 156</th><th>Firefox 155</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>有沒有帶在 myapp.test 登入時拿到的 cookie</td><td>有</td><td>沒有</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>登入 cookie 是使用者逛 myapp.test 的時候拿到的，所以 Firefox 只在使用者逛 myapp.test 時才送它。如果小工具靠這個 cookie 判斷登入，嵌在 other.test 上的時候，在 Firefox 裡就會顯示未登入。</p>
<p>不過使用者如果是點連結過去的，Firefox 會多送一些 cookie。實測時，使用者在 localhost 的頁面點了連結，進到 thembase.localhost，接著 thembase.localhost 的頁面對 localhost 發請求。照上面的規則，使用者這時在逛 thembase.localhost，不該帶 localhost 的 cookie，可是 Firefox 155 帶了。沒寫 <code>SameSite</code> 跟 <code>SameSite=None</code> 的 cookie 都帶上了，<code>Lax</code> 跟 <code>Strict</code> 的還是沒帶，因為這個請求仍然算跨站。這個例外只在 *.localhost 上測過。</p>
<p>Firefox 這樣做，應該是為了「用 A 網站的帳號登入 B 網站」這種流程。使用者從 A 點連結到 B，B 的頁面要向 A 問這個人有沒有登入，如果請求沒帶 A 的 cookie，A 只會回答未登入。</p>
<h3>http 跟 https 算不算同站：Schemeful same-site</h3>
<pre><code>網址列：http://myapp.test
GET https://myapp.test/api
→ Cookie: id=abc     Firefox 155（cookie 是 SameSite=Lax）
→ （沒有 Cookie）     Chrome 156
</code></pre>
<p>網域一樣，只有頁面是 http、請求是 https。判斷兩邊是不是同站的時候，Chrome 從 91 版開始連 scheme（http 還是 https）也一起比，所以這個請求在 Chrome 算跨站，<code>Lax</code> 跟 <code>Strict</code> 的 cookie 都不帶。Firefox 只比 eTLD+1，算同站。這個改動叫 <a href="https://web.dev/articles/schemeful-samesite">Schemeful Same-Site</a>。如果整個網站都走 HTTPS，就不會碰到這種情況。</p>
<h2>為什麼 SameSite=None 一定要加 Secure</h2>
<p><code>SameSite=None</code> 的 cookie 在跨站請求也會送，送出去的次數多很多。如果沒有 <code>Secure</code>，它也會走純 HTTP，同一個咖啡店 Wi-Fi 上的人就能直接從網路上讀到它。所以有執行這條規則的瀏覽器，會直接拒收這種 cookie：</p>
<pre><code>Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=None             拒收，沒有 Secure
Set-Cookie: id=abc; SameSite=None; Secure     收下，只在 HTTPS 送出
</code></pre>
<p>Chrome 從 Chrome 80 開始執行，Firefox 到 Firefox 131 才跟上，Safari 沒有執行（<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie#browser_compatibility">MDN 相容性資料</a>）。實測 Chrome 156、Firefox 151 跟 155 都拒收沒有 <code>Secure</code> 的 <code>SameSite=None</code>。</p>
<h2>目前最佳組合</h2>
<pre><code>Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
</code></pre>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>HttpOnly</code></strong>：頁面上的 JavaScript 從 <code>document.cookie</code> 讀不到它，XSS payload 就沒辦法把 session ID 抄出去。不過 XSS 還是能從頁面發請求，瀏覽器照樣會幫這些請求帶上 cookie。</li>
<li><strong><code>Secure</code></strong>：只走 HTTPS。Chrome 跟 Firefox 在 <code>http://localhost</code> 上也收。</li>
<li><strong><code>SameSite=Lax</code></strong>：明寫出來，因為只有 Chrome 預設是它。</li>
<li><strong><code>Path=/</code></strong>：整個 app。</li>
</ul>
<p>只有 subdomain 真的需要共用 cookie 時才加 <code>Domain</code>。加了之後每一個 subdomain 都收得到，別的團隊、別的程式跑的 subdomain 也一樣。</p>
